newsitem.title: USA: Clinton said warming to Gingrich budget offer.
newsitem.headline: Clinton said warming to Gingrich budget offer.

text.p: President Clinton has offered to delay action on his proposed tuition tax credits and other tax cuts to boost the chance of reaching a budget accord with the Republican-led Congress, the Washington Post reported in Sunday editions.

White House Chief of Staff Erskine Bowles informed a number of key Democrats in Congress last week that the president would be willing to forgo his proposals for cutting taxes if Republicans would do the same, the newspaper said.
House Speaker Newt Gingrich angered some Republicans this past week by suggesting that Republicans could postone their proposed tax cuts for now in order to secure a balanced budget deal.
House Minority Leader Richard Gephardt Saturday told CNN he would be willing to consider delaying tax cuts in order to pass a balanced budget.
"I'm willing to look at it. I haven't really decided the question," Gephardt said, when asked about Gingrich's suggestion.
He called on Republicans to speed up the pace of their work on the budget, adding faster progress could happen if they made a commitment to bipartisan efforts.
Senior administration officials told the Post Clinton would push to enact tax cuts later in the year if Republicans agreed to delay the cuts to secure a balanced budget.

"The president is committed to enacting his tax cut and balancing the budget, and he believes his budget plan shows you can do both," the Post quoted Gene Sperling, chairman of Clinton's National Economic Council, as saying.
"But if having a separate vote on tax cuts turns out to be means of getting a bipartisan balanced budget agreement, we're open to that," he said.
Clinton initially hailed Gingrich's suggestion as "encouraging" but he carefully avoided any suggestion that he might be willing to reciprocate by backing away from his own proposed tax cuts.
As part of his fiscal 1998 budget, Clinton proposed $98 billion in tax cuts over the next five years, including a tuition tax credit and a $500-per-child break for middle-income families.
The budget would partially offset the lost revenue with a package of $78 billion in tax and fee increases, mostly aimed at businesses and investors.
Republicans were pushing for tax cuts ranging up to $201 billion.
Gephardt said the time had come for genuine bipartisan efforts to pass the budget.

"The way we used to do things is the committee would meet, Republicans and Democrats together, and they would work together to try to produce a budget. That's what we ought to be doing now -- not putting up trial balloons," he said.
